note: IMPORTANT, commonly confused distinction: 'vitro'/vitrocerámica is a RADIANT electric hob — a resistive coil heats the ceramic glass, which then conducts heat into the pan. It is NOT induction, despite both having a flat glass-look surface and often being confused as the same thing: induction heats the pan directly via a magnetic field (much faster response, works only with ferromagnetic cookware, not modeled as a separate entity here since it wasn't asked about). Vitro's 'slow' response is real, physical thermal lag: the glass and coil have real thermal mass, so turning the dial down does NOT reduce delivered heat immediately the way closing a gas valve does — the surface stays hot and keeps transferring heat for a real, noticeable period after being turned down. This is the single most commonly-experienced practical difference from gas: overshooting a target temperature is easy on vitro precisely because the feedback loop a cook is used to (turn it down, heat drops now) doesn't hold the same way.
